newsitem.title: USA: Battle over low gasoline inventories simmers.
newsitem.headline: Battle over low gasoline inventories simmers.

text.p: Girding for another battle this spring over gasoline prices, the oil industry Wednesday said low inventories were not the cause of high gasoline prices, but that high crude oil prices were to blame.
With gasoline inventories down 3 percent from this time last year, consumer advocates have already started raising concern about another potential price spike this spring like last year's.

But Edward Murphy, director of statistics for the American Petroleum Institute, said if oil companies were forced to put more product into storage to bolster stocks ahead of the driving season, there would be less on the market to meet current demand, and drivers would have to pay even more.
"The inventory drawdown was one that was necessitated by an imbalance between demand and supply," Murphy told a news conference where API released its annual supply and demand data.
"Worldwide supply of crude has not kept up with increased demand," he said. "It's the crude oil price increases that are driving up the gasoline prices."
Total U.S. petroleum demand grew by a strong 2.8 percent in 1996 from 1995, compared with average growth of 1.5 percent over the previous three years, API said.
While acknowledging that petroleum inventories were heavily depleted over the last 18 months, Murphy said the low stock levels did not indicate a trend.
"I don't think we can look at what happened in the last 18 months and say this is a change in inventory behaviour," he said.
Other analysts said whether the lower stock levels were long term or not, they were a current reality that added volatility to the market.

"As long as refiners are keeping lower inventories, it gives an enormous amount of power to speculators," said Sarah Emerson, a director of Energy Security Analysis Inc., a Washington-based consulting firm.
Seeing inventories so low, speculators say: "'What a good reason to buy crude,'" she said.
Consumer advocate Ed Rothschild of Citizen Action said gasoline stocks should be closely watched at the end of February or March.
"If there's no build to at least where we were in late March or early April 1996, we're going to see a rise above where we were in May 1996," he said.

Gasoline prices peaked last year in May at $1.32. Current gasoline prices at around $1.28 are 17 cents, or 13 percent, above this time last year. But crude oil prices are $7, or almost 40 percent, above year-ago levels, according to Energy Department statistics.
Emerson said prices were higher for several reasons, including strong demand, lower-than-anticipated crude supplies from non-OPEC sources, and low inventories.

As long as oil companies sought to cut operating costs by keeping lean inventories, demand for gasoline would have to fall and a "giant wave of crude oil" would have to come on the market in order to bring prices down substantially, she said.
